newsitem.title: USA: California slaps Chrysler with car shipment ban.
newsitem.headline: California slaps Chrysler with car shipment ban.

text.p: In a blow to Chrysler Corp. aimed at quashing "lemon law" violations, California's Department of Motor Vehicles Thursday banned the automaker from shipping new vehicles to dealers in the state for 45 days.
The decision could dent Chrysler's sales in the nation's largest car and truck market.

But the ban, which would take effect on Nov. 25, would not put the automaker's 240 California dealers out of business, allowing them to continue to sell cars already on their lots and to service vehicles.

Chrysler, which has steadfastly denied any wrongdoing, said it plans to appeal, which could drag the process out for years. The company sold 169,800 new cars and trucks in California during 1995, about 7.8 percent of its total volume, according to R.L. Polk & Co.

In May, an administrative law judge found Chrysler guilty of 116 violations of the state's Lemon Law, citing the automaker's failure to notify used car customers that the vehicles they were buying were returned by their original owners because of chronic problems.
At the time, Judge Keith Levy had recommended a 60-day suspension but the agency reduced it to 45 days after dealers complained the penalty would seriously hurt their business.

"The action taken today is taken against Chrysler Corporation, not corporation dealerships in California," Department of Motor Vehicles Director Sally Reed said. "Prohibiting the restocking of vehicles for 45 days, coupled with other sanctions, sends the strongest message to Chrysler Corporation, but should have less effect on innocent parties."

The agency banned Chrysler from re-selling so-called "Lemon Law" buybacks and re-selling good-will repurchases within the state for three years and put the No. 3 U.S. automaker on probation for three years.

Under the state's lemon law, an automaker must buy back a car from a first owner if it spends 30 days in a repair shop during first year of ownership, or if specific problem hasn't been fixed after three attempts.
Consumer advocates quickly praised the decision.

"This is the equivalent of putting a corporation behind bars by taking them off the street," said Clarence Ditlow, a longtime consumer advocate and executive director of the Centre for Auto Safety in Washington, D.C. "It's a landmark day for consumers."
He added that the DMV's penalty was the first action tough enough to deter so-called lemon laundering.

"The only way to stop lemon laundering is to suspend a corporation from doing business. If you fine them, they ignore it, they consider it a cost of doing business and they continue laundering lemons," he said.
In a statement, Chrysler said it planned to appeal the decision to the state's New Motor Vehicle Board, an independent body set up to review regulatory decisions on cars and trucks in California.
Chrysler said the decision will not become effective, if at all, until the appeals process is exhausted.
Industry analysts said they doubted that the ban will ultimately be imposed, and at the very least, Chrysler can buy enough time to ship extra vehicles to build up dealer inventories in California.
Despite the fact that Californians buy about 10 percent of the nation's cars and trucks, analysts said the financial impact of the penatly on Chrysler would be minimal.
"We're talking about rearranging 1 percent of Chrysler's annual U.S. volume," said Burnham Securities analyst David Healy. "You're really punishing car buyers and dealers."
Chrysler said its dealers presented "unrefuted evidence" to the DMV that the penalty will cause them and consumers economic harm.
"The DMV has essentially ignored this evidence of harm to California citizens, just as it ignored evidence of Chrysler's compliance with California law," the company said.
Chrysler spokesman James Crawford said the appeals process could take a long time to complete, and the matter could eventually wind up in a civil courtroom.
"We didn't expect them to ignore all the evidence that they apparently did, but i don't think anyone's surprised by it," he said.

The vehicles in question were sold in 1992. Chrysler contends the cars were sold to dealers at auctions and the automaker supplied a disclosure notice and unlimited 12-month warranty with every vehicle.
